## Introduction

Picking stocks that will go up is hard. Picking stocks that will go down is also hard. Furthermore, listening to what randos on social media say about which stocks will go up or down doesn't seem like a good strategy. Now suppose we do the opposite of what the randos say. Can we make money that way? In, preview, "Yes."

I was struck by [this column](https://www.bloomberg.com/opinion/newsletters/2025-10-14/venture-global-s-gas-plant-is-done) by Matt Levine on Bloomberg which refers to an academic paper by Aaron Kaufman, Jax Li and Nasser Alansari, "StockTwits: Comprehensive records of a financial social media platform from 2008 to 2022."[@Li_Al_Ansari_Kaufman_2025] In it the authors analyze the sentiment of 550 million (!) posts on StockTwits, a social media platform for traders and investors. Please refer to the paper for how the authors did their sentiment analysis. They find that some users do statistically better than guessing and some do statistically worse. The bad pickers have negative "alpha." In this post we well set out to see if we can make money by following what the "good" pickers say and doing the opposite of what the "bad" pickers say whether their sentiment is bullish or bearish.

::: callout-note
## Kudos!

I commend the authors of the paper for providing access to the complete data set and some sample python code so that other researchers might replicate their results. This is how all academic publishing should look like. You can access the [code and instructions](https://github.com/Jaxingjili/StockTwits-from-2008-to-2022) for accessing the data on Github.
:::

## The plan

First we need to access the data which is stored as a number of CSV format files in an Amazon AWS S3 bucket. These are freely available public files. They take up gigabytes of storage so do not want to bring them all into memory at once. I recommend using DuckDB to manage the data since it lets us work with datasets larger than what will fit in memory.

There are over 500 million posts in the total data set but the study authors have used sentiment analysis to identify those posts which have both a stock ticker symbol and a bullish or bearish sentiment. This reduces the data set to about 100 million posts. This is the dataset we will download. We can further winnow the data so that the users and tickers we analyze have a minimum number of mentions.

![](funnel.jpg)

Using Yahoo Finance we will download the price histories of the most popular stocks in our data set. Then we'll see if we can duplicate the findings of the paper in identifying the existence of statistically good or bad pickers over the whole range of the data.

Finally, we'll see if a trading strategy can be constructed. using out-of-sample data.

## Get The Stocktwits Data

The dataset is stored in a number of different formats, each with varying amounts of information. We are only interested in the files which contain a user ID, ticker symbol and sentiment (bullish or bearish) which is the "symbol_sentiments" dataset, stored as 34 CSV files. The files are public so we don't need any login credentials. The heavy lifting of this project is done by DuckDB and the Duckplyr package in R. DuckDB is an SQL-language database management system which can handle very large datasets efficiently without necessarily loading them in memory all at once. Duckplyr is a package which allows us to use the dplyr syntax we know and love while DuckDB is the back end. In theory, you don't even need to download the files locally but I found that downloading them first and then pointing DuckDB to the local files is much faster in practice. The files will take up about one GB of disk space.

```{r load libraries}
#| code-fold: true
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(duckdb)
library(duckplyr)
library(gt)
```

```{r download data}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true

# Create DuckDB connection with S3 support
con <- dbConnect(duckdb())

# Tell DuckDB we are getting files from S3 in us-west-2 region
dbExecute(con, "INSTALL httpfs;")
dbExecute(con, "LOAD httpfs;")
dbExecute(con, "SET s3_region='us-west-2';")

BASE_URL <- "https://stocktwits-nyu.s3.amazonaws.com/dataset/v1/data/csv/"
DATASET <- "symbol_sentiments"
STEM_URL <- paste0(BASE_URL, DATASET, "/", DATASET, "_")
# make data subdirectory if it doesn't exist
if (!dir.exists("data")) dir.create("data")
get_sentiment_file <- function(file_num) {
  file_num_str <- sprintf("%02d", file_num)
  csv_url <- paste0(STEM_URL, file_num_str, ".csv")
  parquet_filename <- paste0("data/", DATASET, "_", file_num_str, ".parquet")
  # Read CSV directly from S3 using DuckDB's HTTP support
  query <- paste0("SELECT * FROM read_csv_auto('", csv_url, "')")
  # Execute query and get as duckplyr dataframe
  df <- dbGetQuery(con, query) |>
    as_duckdb_tibble() |>
    compute_parquet(parquet_filename)
  print(paste(parquet_filename,format(file.info(parquet_filename)$size),"bytes") )
}
# there are 34 csv files in the S3 bucket for symbol_sentiments
walk(0:33, get_sentiment_file)
```

If all goes well we'll have 34 parquet-format files in a 'data' subfolder . Now comes the fun part, data cleaning. Each post might mention multiple tickers so we need to explode the data so that each row contains only one ticker symbol. We can then see that some users might post multiple times about the same ticker on the same day, trying to hype the stock in real time. I think one mention per user per ticker per day will suffice.

::: callout-tip
I prefer to use the Dplyr vernacular when working in R. When using any large data frame, I recommend using a Duckplyr/DuckDB/Parquet-files workflow. Duckplyr is a package which translates Dplyr verbs into SQL queries executed by DuckDB. This allows you to work with datasets larger than memory without having to learn SQL. If you are familiar with Dplyr, Duckplyr will feel very natural. Parquet is a column-oriented file stroage format suited for large datasets.

There is a notion that if you can fit a dataset into memory, a database like DuckDB is not a time saver. I disagree. Further, Duckplyr is the best database frontend package for R. You see my discussion on the relative performance of database packages [here](https://outsiderdata.netlify.app/posts/2024-04-10-the-truth-about-tidy-wrappers/benchmark_wrappers).

When using Duckplyr, operations are "lazy". Nothing is actually computed until necessary. This allows you to chain together multiple operations without having to create intermediate datasets. Do use Duckplyr's verbs where possible to take advantage of this feature. For instance, if you want to query the size of the dataset, use `summarise()` rather than `nrow()`. The former will compute a single-row data frame, while the latter will pull the entire dataset into memory.
:::

```{r clean data}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
cat("Loading sentiment data...\n")
sentiments <- duckplyr::read_parquet_duckdb( "data/symbol_sentiments_*.parquet" )
summarise(sentiments, n = n())

# use only necessary columns and convert types to save memory
sentiments <- sentiments |>
  select(-message_id) |>
  mutate(user_id = as.integer(user_id)) |>
  # convert sentiment to boolean within duckplyr to save some space
  # not bullish  means bearish
  mutate(bullish = sentiment == 1) |>
  select(-sentiment)
# expand python-like symbol_list into multiple rows. This will take some time.
cat("Expanding posts mentioning multiple tickers...\n")
sentiments <- sentiments |>
  mutate(symbol_list = gsub("\\[|\\]|'| ", "", symbol_list)) |>
  collect() |>
  separate_longer_delim(symbol_list, delim = ",") |>
  as_duckdb_tibble() |>
  # retain only rows with valid symbols (A-Z, 1-5 characters)
  filter(grepl("^[A-Z]{1,5}$", symbol_list)) |>
  rename(date = created_at, ticker = symbol_list)

# when people post multiple messages about the same ticker on the same day, filter out.
sentiments <- sentiments |>
  distinct(user_id, ticker, date, bullish, .keep_all = TRUE)  |> 
  # save cleaned data
  compute_parquet("data/sentiments_cleaned.parquet")

summarise(sentiments, n = n())
```

So far we have winnowed the data set down to roughly 50 million rows. Ultimately, we will create sliding window sample sets and we want to have a valid sample size in each window. Accordingly, we can filter out posts that are not likely to be statistically useful. While somewhat arbitrary, let's limit the number of stocks to the 500 top-mentioned common stock tickers and keep only the user IDs that have posted more than 100 times and were active for more than six months. Note we have omitted cryptocurrencies, which are also popular on StockTwits.

```{r filter sentiments}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
MIN_POSTS <- 100
MIN_DAYS <- 180 # were they active over at least 6 months
NUM_TICKERS <- 500

# determine the most popular tickers
popular_tickers <- sentiments |>
summarise(
    .by = ticker,
    count = n(),
    start_date = min(date),
    end_date = max(date)
    )   |>
  arrange(desc(count)) |>
  slice_head(n=NUM_TICKERS) |> 
  # save popular tickers to download price data later
compute_parquet("data/popular_tickers.parquet")

# include only the most popular tickers
sentiments <- popular_tickers |>
  select(ticker) |>
  inner_join(sentiments, by = "ticker")

summarise(sentiments, n = n())

# only include user_ids with at least 200 entries
sentiments <- sentiments |>
  summarise(
    .by = user_id,
    date_range = max(date) - min(date),
    count = n()
  ) |>
  inner_join((sentiments), by = "user_id")
summarise(sentiments, n = n())

sentiments <- sentiments |>
  filter(count >= MIN_POSTS, date_range >= MIN_DAYS) |>
  select(-date_range, -count)

summarise(sentiments, n = n())

compute_parquet(sentiments, "data/sentiments_filtered.parquet")
```

What we have now is a dataset where each post has a unique user ID, ticker, post date and sentiment. Where sentiment is TRUE for bullish and FALSE for bearish.

```{r show sample posts}
#| code-fold: true
sentiments <- read_parquet_duckdb("data/sentiments_filtered.parquet")

slice_head(sentiments, n = 10) |> 
  collect() |> 
  gt::gt() |> 
  # add title
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Sample StockTwits Posts After Cleaning and Filtering"
  )
```

Looking at the most popular tickers we see a mix of large cap stocks like AAPL, TSLA and AMZN, meme stocks like GME , NIO and AMC, along with SPY, the S&P 500 index.

```{r show popular tickers}
#| code-fold: true
popular_tickers <- read_parquet_duckdb("data/popular_tickers.parquet")
head(popular_tickers,n=10) |> 
  gt::gt() |>  
  # add title
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Most Popular StockTwits Tickers"
  ) |> 
  gt::fmt_number(
    columns = c(count),
    decimals = 0
  )
```

Interestingly, like Charles Dickens and earthquakes, the relative frequency of top ticker mentions follows [Zipf's law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zipf%27s_law), where the rank of mentions varies logarithmically with the number of mentions. This is indicative of a "[preferential attachment process](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Preferential_attachment)". The Stocktwits like to pile on, in other words.

```{r show zipfs law}
#| code-fold: true
#| message: false
# show popular tickers on a log/log frequency plot
popular_tickers <- popular_tickers |>
  arrange(desc(count)) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number())
popular_tickers |>
  ggplot(aes(x = rank, y = count)) +
  geom_point() +
  scale_x_log10(limits = c(1,1000)) +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  # add labels for top 10 tickers
  geom_text(
    data = popular_tickers |> slice_head(n = 10),
    aes(label = ticker),
    vjust = -1,
    size = 3
  ) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = FALSE, color = "blue") +
  labs( 
    title = "Popularity Begets Popularity",
    subtitle = "Rank Frequency Plot of Top 500 StockTwits Ticker Mentions",
    x = "Rank of Ticker by Mentions (log scale)",
    y = "Number of Mentions (log scale)"
  )
```

## Download Price Data

Now let's download price data for the popular tickers for the date windows where they are mentioned in the StockTwits posts. We can get historical price data from Yahoo Finance. While we will search for the 500 top tickers, some tickers may not be found on Yahoo Finance. We'll skip those tickers.

```{r }
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
library(yahoofinancer)
# function to download prices
ticker_hist <- function(ticker, start_date, end_date, interval_pd = "1d") {
  ticker_obj <- Ticker$new(ticker)
  px_hist <- ticker_obj$get_history(
    interval = interval_pd,
    start = start_date,
    end = end_date + 7 # buffer to include week after last mention
  )  |>  
    mutate(date = as.Date(date))
  return(px_hist)
}
# we saved  popular tickers earlier
popular_tickers <- read_parquet_duckdb("data/popular_tickers.parquet")
all_prices <- list()
start_row <- 1
for (i in start_row:nrow(popular_tickers)) {
  ticker <- popular_tickers$ticker[i]
  start_date <- popular_tickers$start_date[i]
  end_date <- popular_tickers$end_date[i]
  print(paste( "Downloading prices for", ticker, "from", start_date,"to", end_date))
  prices <- ticker_hist(ticker, start_date, end_date)
  # Check if API request failed
  if (is.null(prices) || nrow(prices) == 0) {
    print(paste("Error: Failed to download prices for", ticker))
    next # Skip to next ticker
  }
    all_prices[[ticker]] <- prices
}
# combine all prices into a single data frame and save
prices_df <- bind_rows(all_prices, .id = "ticker") |> 
  duckplyr::compute_parquet(prices_df, "price_history_top500.parquet")
```

::: callout-note
Tidyverse experts will question why I used a `for()` loop instead of the `purrr::map()` function. When getting data from an external source, I don't want to lose progress if one of the calls fails in a way I didn't anticipate. Using a for loop lets me fix the error and resume from the last successful call by manually setting the start index rather than having to start over.
:::

We can make a couple interesting observations about the prices. Most of the most popular tickers are meme stocks and many of the adjusted close prices are absurdly high, millions of dollars per share. This is not an error. Most meme stocks have been relentless destroyers of value. To boost the nominal dollar share price, companies will do a reverse split, sometimes many reverse splits. The adjusted close price keeps continuity where there would otherwise be a gap jump in the share price. This has the effect of making it appear that historical share prices are higher than they were at the time are but allows accurate return calculations over long time periods.

Second, the volatility of these meme stocks is crazy. Wherever this exercise takes us, we know were are in for a wild ride. TSLA, the most volatile of the mega cap stocks AND a popular meme stock, is one of the less volatile stocks in our sample.


```{r show vol histogram}

prices_df <- read_parquet_duckdb("data/price_history_top500.parquet") |> 
  as_tibble()
price_volatility <- prices_df |>
  arrange(ticker, date) |>
  mutate(
    .by = ticker,
    daily_return = (adj_close / lag(adj_close)) - 1
  ) |>
  summarise(
    .by = ticker,
    volatility = sd(daily_return, na.rm = TRUE) * sqrt(252) # annualized volatility
  ) |>

price_volatility |>

gg <- price_volatility |>

  geom_vline(
    data = price_volatility |> filter(ticker == "SPY"),

    color = "red",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  # add vline for TSLA volatility
  geom_vline(
    data = price_volatility |> filter(ticker == "TSLA"),
    aes(xintercept = volatility),
    color = "blue",
    linetype = "dashed",
    size = 1
  ) +
  # log x scale with percentage labels
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1)) +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of Annualized Volatility of Popular Stocktwits Tickers",
    x = "Annualized Volatility (log scale)",

  ) +
  # label the SPY line
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = price_volatility |> filter(ticker == "SPY") |> pull(volatility) * 1.2,
    y = 9,

      price_volatility |>
        filter(ticker == "SPY") |>

    angle = 90
  ) +
  # label the TSLA line
  annotate(
    "text",
    x = price_volatility |> filter(ticker == "TSLA") |> pull(volatility) * 1.2,
    y = 9,
    label = glue::glue(
      "TSLA ",
      price_volatility |>
        filter(ticker == "TSLA") |>
        pull(volatility) |>

print(gg)
```

Now that we have the prices, we'll build a table of price changes. Take the adjusted close on the date of the post as our starting price. We'll take the adjusted close price one week later as our ending price. Compute the absolute price change and the change relative to SPY so we can test either. 
```{r make price change table}
#| eval: true
#| code-fold: true
price_changes <- prices_df |>
  arrange(ticker, date) |>
  mutate(
    .by = ticker,
    adj_close_lead_w = lead(adj_close, 5),
    adj_change_1w = (adj_close_lead_w - adj_close) / adj_close
  ) |>
  select(ticker, date, adj_change_1w) |>
  # add another column for pct change minus the SPY change
  left_join(
    prices_df |>
      filter(ticker == "SPY") |>
      arrange(date) |>
      mutate(
        .by = ticker,
        adj_close_lead_w = lead(adj_close, 5),
        spy_adj_change_1w = (adj_close_lead_w - adj_close) / adj_close
      ) |>
      select(date, spy_adj_change_1w),
    by = "date"
  ) |>
  mutate(pct_change_minus_spy = adj_change_1w - spy_adj_change_1w) |>
  select(ticker, date, adj_change_1w, pct_change_minus_spy) #

# ticker is SPY then make pct_change_minus_spy equal to adj_change_1w
price_changes <- price_changes |>
  filter(ticker == "SPY") |>
  mutate(pct_change_minus_spy = adj_change_1w) |>
  union_all((price_changes)) |>
  # remove rows where ticker is SPY and pct_change_minus_spy is 0
  filter(!(ticker == "SPY" & pct_change_minus_spy != adj_change_1w))
```

Now match the price changes to the sentiment posts to create a track record. If the direction of the price change matches the sentiment of the post, we count it as a correct prediction. There are two obvious caveats with this approach. We don't know what time horizon the poster had in mind when making the post. It could have been a week, a month or 5 minutes. Second, we assume we transact at the closing prices on the day of the post and one week later, which may not be feasible.
```{r calculate track record}
#| code-fold: true
# TRACK RECORD CALCULATION ==============================
# join popular_sentiments with price_changes
track_record <- sentiments |>
  left_join(price_changes, by = c("ticker", "date")) |>
  #  na.omit() |>
  # add true/false column for whether adj_change_1w  has the same sign as sentiment
  mutate(
    win_absolute = bullish == (adj_change_1w > 0),
    win_vs_SPY = bullish == (pct_change_minus_spy > 0)
  ) |>
  #  select(user_id, ticker, date, bullish, win_absolute)
  select(user_id, ticker, date, bullish, win_absolute, win_vs_SPY) |>
  filter(!is.na(win_absolute) & !is.na(win_vs_SPY)) 
  # make sure we have at least 50 posts per user with matched prices
  
track_record_bull <- track_record |>
  filter(bullish)
track_record_bear <- track_record |>
  filter(!bullish)

track_record |> slice_head(n = 10) |> 
  collect() |> 
  gt::gt() |> 
  # add title
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Sample Track Record Entries"
  )
```

Once we have the track records we can compute the batting average for each user.
```{r compute win rates}
#| code-fold: true
# compute win rate by user_id
get_win_rate <- function(track_record, abs_or_rel = c("relative", "absolute")) {
  if (abs_or_rel == "relative") {
    user_win_rate <- summarise(
      track_record,
      .by = user_id,
      total = n(),
      wins = sum(win_vs_SPY),
      win_rate = sum(win_vs_SPY) / n()
    )
  } else {
    {
      user_win_rate <- summarise(
        track_record,
        .by = user_id,
        total = n(),
        wins = sum(win_absolute),
        win_rate = sum(win_absolute) / n()
      )
    } |>
      arrange(desc(win_rate)) |>
      filter(!is.na(win_rate))
  }
  return(user_win_rate)
}
user_win_rate <- get_win_rate(track_record, "relative")
bear_win_rate <- get_win_rate(track_record_bear, "relative")
bull_win_rate <- get_win_rate(track_record_bull, "relative")
methods_restore()
bull_win_rate |> 
  arrange(desc(win_rate)) |> 
  filter(total >= 50) |>
  slice_head(n=10) |> 
  collect() |> 
  gt::gt() |> 
  # add title
  gt::tab_header(
    title = "Top 10 Batting Averages vs SPY"
  ) |> 
    # add footer
  gt::tab_source_note(
    source_note = "Minimum 50 posts with price matches") |> 
  gt::fmt_percent(
    columns = c(win_rate),
    decimals = 1
  )
```

We are interested in finding the users whose batting averages are statistically signficant so we'll use a binomial test and keep only those users who are signficant at the 95% level.
```{r test significance}
#| eval: false
#| code-fold: true
# Perform binomial tests for each user
# H0: p = 0.5 (random chance)
# H1: p ≠ 0.5 (not random chance)

get_significanct_posters <- function(win_rate) {
  results <- win_rate |>
    as_tibble() |>
    rowwise() |>
    mutate(
      # Perform two-sided binomial test
      binom_test = list(binom.test(
        wins,
        total,
        p = 0.5,
        alternative = "two.sided"
      )),
      p_value = binom_test$p.value,
      conf_low = binom_test$conf.int[1],
      conf_high = binom_test$conf.int[2]
    ) |>
    ungroup() |>
    select(-binom_test, -starts_with("conf")) |>
    arrange(p_value)

  # Filter for statistically significant results (p < 0.05)
  significant_posters <- results |>
    filter(p_value < 0.05) |>
    mutate(
      alpha_direction = as.integer(case_when(
        win_rate > 0.5 ~ 1,
        win_rate < 0.5 ~ -1,
        TRUE ~ 0
      ))
    ) |>
    select(-p_value)

  return(significant_posters)
}

# separate bulls from bears and save result
significant_posters <- get_significanct_posters(bear_win_rate) |>
  mutate(sentiment = "bearish") |>
  bind_rows(
    get_significanct_posters(bull_win_rate) |>
      mutate(sentiment = "bullish")
  ) |>
  compute_parquet("data/significant_posters.parquet")
```
Stocktwits is filled with retail traders who are generally long-only and trying to hype stocks. It is therefore not surprising that there are far more bullish posts than bearish posts. What is surprising is that there are far more posters with statistically significant negative skill than positive skill. In other words, there are many more bad pickers than good pickers on StockTwits. While there are mostly bullish posts, the bearish posters are more likely to show positive skill.

```{r summary table}
#| code-fold: true
# make a table of the summary using gt with bearish/bullish counts
significant_posters <- 
  read_parquet_duckdb("data/significant_posters.parquet")
 
row1 <- track_record |> 
  mutate(sentiment = if_else(bullish, "bullish", "bearish")) |> 
  summarise(.by = sentiment, n= n())
  
row2 <- significant_posters |> summarise(.by = sentiment, n= n())
row3_4<-significant_posters |> 
  summarise(.by = c(alpha_direction,sentiment), n= n())

#bind rows in a table
detailed_table <- tibble(
  Metric = c(
    "Total posters tested",
    "posters significantly different from chance",
    "posters significantly better than .500",
    "posters significantly worse than .500"
  ),
  Bearish = c(
    pull(filter(row1, sentiment == "bearish"), n),
    pull(filter(row2, sentiment == "bearish"), n),
    pull(filter(row3_4, alpha_direction == 1, sentiment == "bearish"), n),
    pull(filter(row3_4, alpha_direction == -1, sentiment == "bearish"), n)
  ),
  Bullish = c(
    pull(filter(row1, sentiment == "bullish"), n),
    pull(filter(row2, sentiment == "bullish"), n),
    pull(filter(row3_4, alpha_direction == 1, sentiment == "bullish"), n),
    pull(filter(row3_4, alpha_direction == -1, sentiment == "bullish"), n)
  )
  ) |> mutate(Total = Bearish + Bullish)

detailed_table |>
  gt() |>
  tab_header(
    title = "Summary of User Win Rate Statistical Tests"
  ) |>
  fmt_number(
    columns = c(Bearish, Bullish, Total),
    decimals = 0
  ) 
```

```{r match-prices-function, eval=FALSE}
# This computation is intensive, so we'll save the results

# methods_restore()
# prices <- as_tibble(prices)
# sentiments <- as_tibble(sentiments)

get_fut_price <- function(prices, days_ahead){
price_chg <- prices |> 
  transmute(ticker,date,price_t0 = adj_close, future_date = date + days(days_ahead)) |> 
  left_join(prices |> 
      select(ticker, date, price_fut = adj_close),
    by = join_by("ticker", "future_date" == "date")
  ) |> filter(!is.na(price_fut))
  return(price_chg)
}
price_chg <- get_fut_price(prices_df, 7)
price_chg <- anti_join(prices_df,price_chg) |> 
  get_fut_price(8) |> 
  bind_rows(price_chg)
# 3 days should be enough to fill most gaps
price_chg <- anti_join(prices_df,price_chg) |> 
  get_fut_price(9) |> 
  bind_rows(price_chg)
# get indexed value change
price_chg <- price_chg |> 
  mutate(
    wk_return = (price_fut - price_t0) / price_t0
  ) |> 
  select(ticker, date, wk_return)
# add column for return relative to SPY return
# Get SPY returns for the same dates
spy_returns <- price_chg |>
  filter(ticker == "SPY") |>
  select(date, spy_wk_return = wk_return)
# Add excess return column (stock return - SPY return)
price_chg <- price_chg |>
  left_join(spy_returns, by = "date") |>
  mutate(
    excess_return = wk_return - spy_wk_return
  ) |>
  select(ticker, date, wk_return, excess_return)


# Join sentiments with prices on the post date
sentiments_with_returns <- sentiments |>
  left_join(price_chg,by = c("ticker", "date")) |> 
  as_tibble()


sentiment_results <- sentiments_with_returns |>
  mutate(
    # Correct if bullish and outperformed, or bearish and underperformed
    correct = case_when(
      bullish & excess_return > 0 ~ TRUE,
      !bullish & excess_return < 0 ~ TRUE,
      TRUE ~ FALSE
    )
  )

# Save the matched data
compute_parquet(sentiment_results, "data/sentiment_results.parquet")
```

```{r rolling-skill-assessment, eval=FALSE}
# This is computationally intensive, so we'll save the results

# Get unique weeks for evaluation
eval_dates <- sentiment_results |>
  distinct(date) |>
  arrange(date) |>
  mutate(week = floor_date(date, "week")) |>
  distinct(week) |>
  filter(week >= min(week) + months(3))  # Need 3 months of history

# Function to assess user skill based on prior 3 months
assess_rolling_skill <- function(eval_date, data, min_posts = 10, p_threshold = 0.05) {
  # Get data from 3 months prior
  start_date <- eval_date - months(3)
  
  historical_data <- data |>
    filter(date >= start_date, date < eval_date)
  
  if(nrow(historical_data) == 0) return(NULL)
  
  # Calculate user statistics
  user_stats <- historical_data |>
    group_by(user_id) |>
    summarise(
      total_posts = n(),
      correct = sum(correct),
      accuracy = mean(correct),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) |>
    filter(total_posts >= min_posts)
  
  # Statistical testing
  user_stats |>
    rowwise() |>
    mutate(
      p_value = binom.test(correct, total_posts, p = 0.5, 
                           alternative = "two.sided")$p.value,
      significant = p_value < p_threshold,
      skill_direction = case_when(
        significant & accuracy > 0.5 ~ "positive",
        significant & accuracy < 0.5 ~ "negative",
        TRUE ~ "none"
      ),
      eval_date = eval_date
    ) |>
    ungroup() |>
    filter(skill_direction != "none") |>
    select(eval_date, user_id, skill_direction, accuracy, total_posts, p_value)
}

# Apply rolling assessment
rolling_skill_results <- map_df(
  eval_dates$week,
  ~assess_rolling_skill(.x, sentiment_results),
  .progress = TRUE
)

# Save results
compute_parquet(rolling_skill_results, "data/rolling_skill_results.parquet")
```

## Step 5: Trading Strategy Implementation

Now we implement two trading strategies:

1. **Long-Only Strategy**: Only take long positions (buy signals)
2. **Long-Short Strategy**: Take both long and short positions

Both strategies:
- Start with $100,000
- Open positions of $1,000 each
- Maximum 10 position openings per day
- Hold SPY when not in other positions
- Close positions after ~1 week
- No margin, no transaction costs

```{r prepare-trading-signals, eval=FALSE}
# Generate trading signals based on rolling skill assessment

# For each sentiment post, check if the user had identified skill in the prior week

# Generate trading signals based on rolling skill assessment

sentiment_results <- read_parquet_duckdb("data/sentiment_results.parquet")

trading_signals <- sentiment_results |>
  mutate(eval_week = floor_date(date, "week")) |>
  left_join(
    rolling_skill_results |> select(eval_date, user_id, skill_direction),
    by = c("eval_week" = "eval_date", "user_id")
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(skill_direction)) |>
  mutate(
    # Generate signal based on user skill and sentiment
    signal = case_when(
      skill_direction == "positive" & bullish ~ "buy",
      skill_direction == "positive" & !bullish ~ "sell",
      skill_direction == "negative" & bullish ~ "sell",
      skill_direction == "negative" & !bullish ~ "buy",
      TRUE ~ "none"
    )
  ) |>
  filter(signal != "none") |>
  arrange(date, ticker) |>
  select(date, ticker, user_id, bullish, skill_direction, signal, 
         price_t0, price_t7, date_t7, stock_return, excess_return)  |>
  compute_parquet("data/trading_signals.parquet")
```
